episodes: The Birth of the Story
Prologue: Valmiki’s story. The royal-court scene belongs to a later time.
Valmiki asked Narada who embodied virtue, courage and truth. Narada began the story of Rama.
Valmiki
Who is the person who has these qualities?
Narada outlined Rama’s birth, exile, search for Sita, war with Ravana and return to Ayodhya.
Narada
Let me tell you Rama’s story.
On the Tamasa riverbank, a hunter killed a krauncha bird. Hearing its mate’s cries, Valmiki’s grief took the form of verse.
Brahma inspired Valmiki to compose Rama’s story. Through meditation, its events became clear, and he planned the poem.
Brahma
Tell Rama’s life in poetry.
Valmiki taught the poem to Lava and Kusha. Later, the two boys recited Rama’s story before King Rama’s court in Ayodhya.
Ayodhya and Its King
The main story now begins in Dasharatha’s kingdom.
Ayodhya stood beside the Sarayu. Under King Dasharatha, its streets, markets and homes flourished.
Dasharatha consulted his ministers and his teacher Vashishtha. Thoughtful counsel, discipline and his people’s welfare guided the kingdom.
The Wish for a Son
Sumantra first recounts an earlier event in Anga.
Concerned about his family’s future, Dasharatha decided to perform a sacrifice. Sumantra advised inviting Rishyasringa.
Sumantra
Invite Rishyasringa.
Anga had suffered without rain. King Romapada planned to invite Rishyasringa, a young sage raised in the forest.
Women from the city went into the forest as the king’s envoys. They befriended Rishyasringa and offered him fruit and sweets.
After they left, Rishyasringa went looking for them. The women met him again and brought him with them to Anga.
Rain fell when Rishyasringa arrived in Anga. Romapada honoured him, and Shanta married him.
Dasharatha himself travelled to Anga. With Romapada’s consent, Rishyasringa and Shanta accompanied him to Ayodhya and received a warm welcome.
The Sacrifice and the Divine Resolve
Events unfold in the capital and in the realm of the gods.
Rishyasringa and Vashishtha oversaw preparations for the Ashvamedha. The rite was completed north of the Sarayu, with arrangements for guests and attendants.
Rishyasringa began the Putreshti rite for sons. Meanwhile, the gods spoke of Ravana’s oppression: his boon had not sought protection from humans.
Vishnu resolved to be born as a human in Dasharatha’s household and end Ravana’s terror.
A divine figure emerged from the sacrificial fire and gave Dasharatha payasa. The king shared it among his three queens; Sumitra received two portions.
At Brahma’s urging, the gods brought forth vanara heroes. In time, they would help Rama fulfil his task.
The Four Princes
Time passes, from infancy to adolescence.
Kaushalya bore Rama, Kaikeyi Bharata, and Sumitra Lakshmana and Shatrughna. The palace celebrated the births of all four boys.
The brothers grew up studying and training in arms. Rama and Lakshmana were especially close, as were Bharata and Shatrughna.
When the princes were adolescents, Vishwamitra arrived at Dasharatha’s court. The king honoured him and asked the purpose of his visit.
Dasharatha
Revered sage, how may I serve you?
A Father’s Difficult Decision
Rama is described here as not yet sixteen.
Maricha and Subahu were disrupting Vishwamitra’s sacrifice. The sage asked Dasharatha to send Rama to protect it.
Vishwamitra
Send Rama to guard the sacrifice.
Dasharatha feared the demons’ strength and Rama’s young age. He offered to go with his army instead.
Dasharatha
Rama is not even sixteen yet.
Vishwamitra was displeased when the king drew back. Vashishtha urged Dasharatha to keep his promise: Vishwamitra could protect and teach Rama.
Vashishtha
Your Majesty, keep the promise you made.
Dasharatha accepted Vashishtha’s counsel. He blessed Rama and Lakshmana and sent them with Vishwamitra.
The First Forest Journey
The present-day journey leads from Ayodhya into the forest.
Beside the Sarayu, Vishwamitra taught Rama Bala and Atibala, disciplines that protected against hunger, fatigue and weakness.

Sages welcomed them near the river confluence. Vishwamitra explained that Kamadeva had tried to disturb Shiva’s meditation here. Shiva’s anger reduced him to ashes; the region was called Anga after the loss of his body.
While crossing the Ganga, Rama asked about the confluence’s roar. Beyond it lay the ruined Malada and Karusha lands, where Vishwamitra described Tataka’s terror.
Rama
What is that roaring sound, revered sage?
Tataka’s Forest
The princes face their first difficult confrontation.
Vishwamitra explained that Tataka was a yaksha maiden, Sunda’s wife and Maricha’s mother. After a curse, she spread violence through this forest.
Rama first wished to restrain Tataka rather than kill her. Vishwamitra explained the prince’s duty to protect the people.
Rama
First, I will restrain her power.
Hearing the bowstring, Tataka rushed at them. She hurled dust and stones, and both brothers faced her attack.
The sage urged Rama to end the danger before dusk. Rama’s arrow killed Tataka, freeing the forest from her terror.
The Weapons and Siddhashrama
Power is accompanied by a lesson in restraint.
Pleased with Rama, Vishwamitra taught him the divine weapons. Rama received the knowledge humbly.
Rama asked how to recall the weapons as well as release them. The sage taught him how to withdraw their power.
Rama
How can these weapons be recalled?
In the hermitage’s history, Vishwamitra told of Vamana: Vishnu asked Bali for three paces of land, then measured the worlds in a vast form.
This was Siddhashrama. Rama and Lakshmana received the sages’ greetings and prepared to guard the sacrifice.
Guarding the Sacrifice
Six days and nights of watchfulness.
Vishwamitra observed silence as the sacrifice began. Rama and Lakshmana kept careful watch for six days and nights.
On the last day, Maricha and Subahu attacked. Rama’s Manava weapon hurled Maricha far toward the sea; he survived.
Subahu continued the attack. Rama struck him down and drove away the remaining attackers.
The sacrifice was completed without further disturbance. The sages praised the brothers, and Vishwamitra expressed his satisfaction.
Vishwamitra
You have protected the sacrifice.
The Road to Mithila and Stories of Old
On the journey, Vishwamitra recounts his family’s past.
The sages were travelling to Janaka’s sacrifice in Mithila. Wishing to see Shiva’s bow, Rama and Lakshmana went with them.
Resting beside the Shona river, Vishwamitra told of Kusha and his four sons. One of them was King Kushanabha.
Kushanabha’s hundred daughters said they would not accept Vayu’s marriage proposal without their father’s consent. In anger, Vayu distorted their bodies. This was an injustice done to them.
The daughters told their father what had happened. Kushanabha praised their patience and gave them affection and support.
The daughters married the righteous Brahmadatta. According to the story, their bodies became healthy again at the wedding.
Kushanabha’s son Gadhi was Vishwamitra’s father. The sage also spoke of his sister Satyavati and her form as the Kaushiki river.
Ganga and Kartikeya
A divine story told beside the Ganga.
At the Ganga, Rama asked how she flowed through the three worlds. The sage began the story of Himavan’s daughters, Ganga and Uma.
Rama
How does Ganga flow through all three worlds?
Ganga went to the gods’ realm, and Uma married Shiva. The gods’ intervention distressed Uma; Agni bore the divine energy.
Through Agni and Ganga, that energy reached the reed forest of Sharavana. Kumara was born there, and six Krittikas cared for him.
Nurtured by the six Krittikas, Kumara was known as the six-faced Shanmukha and as Kartikeya. The gods appointed him their commander.
Sagara’s Sons and the Missing Horse
Vishwamitra tells the story of Rama’s ancestors.
King Sagara had children by two queens: Asamanjasa by Keshini, and sixty thousand sons by Sumati. Asamanjasa was exiled for his cruel conduct.
Indra took the horse from Sagara’s sacrifice. To complete the rite, the king sent his sons to find it.
Unable to find the horse, the sons dug into the earth, distressing many creatures. Their search brought them to Kapila’s hermitage.
Mistaking Kapila for the thief, the sons tried to attack him. The radiance of his anger reduced them to ashes.
After a long wait, Sagara sent his grandson Anshuman. He found the horse and his uncles’ ashes, then searched for water for their rites.
Garuda explained that only Ganga’s water could bring them deliverance. Anshuman returned with the horse, and Sagara completed the sacrifice.
Garuda
They need the waters of Ganga.
Bhagiratha and Ganga’s Descent
Generations pass before Bhagiratha takes up the task.
After Sagara, neither Anshuman nor Dilipa could bring Ganga down. Dilipa’s son Bhagiratha resolved to complete the task.
Pleased by Bhagiratha’s austerities, Brahma explained that the earth could not withstand Ganga’s force. Shiva’s help was needed.
Brahma
Only Shiva can bear Ganga’s force.
Bhagiratha won Shiva’s favour. As Ganga descended, Shiva caught her powerful flow in his matted locks.
At Bhagiratha’s prayer, Shiva released Ganga. Her waters divided into seven streams, and one followed Bhagiratha.
Ganga’s rushing waters flooded Jahnu’s sacrificial ground. The angry sage drank up the river, stopping her flow.
At the gods’ request, Jahnu released Ganga again. Through this connection she also became known as Jahnavi, and continued onward.
Ganga’s water reached the ashes of Sagara’s sons, bringing them deliverance. Bhagiratha performed the rites for his ancestors.
Brahma praised Bhagiratha’s effort. Vishwamitra ended the story, and Rama and Lakshmana prepared to continue their journey.
The Churning of the Ocean and Vishala
Another ancient story on the road to Vishala.
Near Vishala, Vishwamitra told how the gods and daityas had joined together to churn the ocean for the nectar of immortality.
Mount Mandara was the churning rod and Vasuki the rope. When the mountain began to sink, Vishnu supported it in his tortoise form.
Deadly Halahala poison emerged from the churning. Seeing the worlds in danger, Shiva bore the poison and averted destruction.
Dhanvantari, the apsaras, Varuni and the nectar emerged. The gods and daityas quarrelled over the nectar.
With Vishnu’s help, the gods received the nectar and prevailed in the struggle. The story then turned to Diti’s grief.
Diti and the Maruts
A wish for revenge gives way to reconciliation.
Grieving the loss of her sons, Diti wished for a son who could defeat Indra. Kashyapa prescribed a strict vow.
Fearing for his life, Indra served Diti while watching for an opportunity. When she faltered in her vow, he divided the unborn child into seven parts.
Diti asked that the seven parts become the Marut deities. Indra agreed, and they reached a reconciliation.
King Vishala had founded a city in this region. His descendant Sumati welcomed Vishwamitra and the two princes.
Ahalya’s Hermitage
On the present journey, the travellers hear Gautama and Ahalya’s earlier story.
Beyond Vishala, they found a deserted hermitage. Vishwamitra explained that Gautama and Ahalya had once lived there.
Rama
Why is this hermitage so deserted?
Indra approached Ahalya disguised as Gautama. She recognized him but accepted him. When Gautama returned, he angrily cursed them both.
Ahalya was to remain unseen and practise penance. The curse would end when Rama arrived.
Rama and Lakshmana entered the hermitage, and Ahalya became visible. They honoured her, and she welcomed her guests.
Gautama returned and was reunited with Ahalya. After receiving their blessings, Vishwamitra and the brothers continued toward Mithila.
Mithila and Shatananda
Shatananda begins the story of Vishwamitra’s earlier life.
In Mithila, King Janaka welcomed Vishwamitra. The sage introduced Rama and Lakshmana and described their protection of the sacrifice.
Janaka’s priest Shatananda was Gautama and Ahalya’s son. He rejoiced to hear that his mother’s curse had ended.
Shatananda
Was my mother’s hospitality accepted?
Shatananda began telling Rama about his teacher’s past. Vishwamitra had once been a king; through austerity and self-restraint, he became a great sage.
King Kaushika and Shabala
Shatananda’s account of Vishwamitra’s past continues.
King Vishwamitra reached Vashishtha’s hermitage with his army. With Shabala’s help, Vashishtha provided food for everyone.
Seeing Shabala’s power, the king wanted her and offered wealth. Vashishtha explained that the cow sustained his hermitage’s work.
Vashishtha
I cannot give Shabala away.
The king tried to take Shabala by force. She returned to Vashishtha and asked for help; the sage allowed her to defend herself.
Armies brought forth by Shabala defeated the king’s forces. Many of his sons also died, leaving Vishwamitra in grief and anger.
Through austerities, Vishwamitra obtained divine weapons from Shiva. He returned to attack Vashishtha’s hermitage in revenge.
Vashishtha’s Brahmadanda staff neutralized every weapon. The king understood that spiritual discipline held greater power than force of arms.
After his defeat, Vishwamitra turned from pride in royal power to rigorous austerity. He sought to become a Brahmarshi.
Vishwamitra
I will now follow the path of austerity and restraint.
The Story of Trishanku
Shatananda’s account of the past continues.
After his austerities, Vishwamitra was called a Rajarshi, but he aspired further. Meanwhile, King Trishanku wished to enter heaven in his own body.
Vashishtha refused to perform this rite. Trishanku then approached his sons, whose curse changed the king’s appearance.
Having lost his support, Trishanku came to Vishwamitra. The sage heard his plight and promised to help.
Trishanku
I have come to you for refuge.
Vishwamitra invited sages to the sacrifice. Some mocked it and refused to come; in anger, he cursed them too.
The sacrifice raised Trishanku upward, but Indra sent him back. Falling headfirst, he called to Vishwamitra.
Trishanku
Revered sage, protect me!
Vishwamitra stopped his fall and began creating new stars. After an agreement with the gods, Trishanku remained in that heavenly position.
Shunahshepa Is Saved
A boy’s prayers and the protection of his life.
Indra took King Ambarisha’s sacrificial animal. The priests demanded a substitute, placing a boy’s life in danger.
After speaking with Richika and his family, Ambarisha took their middle son Shunahshepa with him. The boy feared being sacrificed in the rite.
At Pushkara, Shunahshepa sought refuge with his relative Vishwamitra. He described his helplessness between his parents’ and the king’s decisions.
Shunahshepa
Revered sage, please save my life.
Vishwamitra’s sons refused to take the boy’s place. The angry sage cursed them, then taught Shunahshepa prayers for protection.
At the sacrifice, Shunahshepa recited the prayers. Pleased, Indra granted him a long life. Ambarisha’s rite was completed, and the boy was saved.
Mastery of the Mind
Vishwamitra’s austerity turns from outward power toward self-restraint.
The apsara Menaka came to Lake Pushkara. Vishwamitra turned from his austerities and spent years with her, then realized he had strayed from his goal.
Vishwamitra peacefully sent Menaka away and resumed his austerities. Even after becoming a Maharshi, he sought complete mastery of his senses.
Indra sent Rambha to disturb his penance. Vishwamitra recognized the attempt and cursed her, but his anger also diminished his spiritual merit.
Vishwamitra understood that he had yet to conquer anger. He undertook a rigorous vow of silence and patience.
Vishwamitra
I must overcome my anger too.
Indra came disguised as a Brahmin and asked for food. Vishwamitra gave away his entire meal and continued his austerities without anger.
At last, Brahma declared him a Brahmarshi, and Vashishtha acknowledged him too. Shatananda’s story ended; Rama was now to see Shiva’s bow.
Shiva’s Bow and Sita
We return to present-day Mithila.
Janaka recounted the history of Shiva’s bow, treasured by his family. The gods had entrusted it to his ancestor Devarata.
Janaka explained that he had found Sita while ploughing the sacrificial ground. He raised her as his daughter and named her Sita.
Janaka had resolved that Sita would marry the one who could string the bow. Earlier kings had failed; their subsequent attack also failed.
Attendants brought the heavy bow. With Vishwamitra’s permission, Rama reached forward to examine, lift and string it.
Vishwamitra
Rama, my child, look at this bow.
Rama lifted and strung the bow with ease. As he drew it, it broke; the resounding crash stunned the assembly.
Janaka proposed Sita’s marriage to Rama. With Vishwamitra’s consent, he sent messengers to invite Dasharatha.
Janaka
I will give Sita in marriage to Rama.
The Marriage Invitation
The families of Ayodhya and Mithila come together.
The messengers reached Ayodhya with news of the broken bow, the princes’ well-being and Janaka’s marriage proposal.
Dasharatha consulted his teachers and ministers. With their agreement, he set out for Mithila with Bharata, Shatrughna and the royal family.
Janaka welcomed Dasharatha to Mithila. The king reunited with his two sons, and wedding preparations moved forward.
Two Families, Four Marriages
The families introduce their lineages and agree to the marriages.
Janaka summoned his brother Kushadhvaja. Vashishtha recounted Rama’s lineage, from Ikshvaku to Dasharatha.
Janaka traced his own family from Nimi. He proposed Sita for Rama and his other daughter Urmila for Lakshmana.
Vishwamitra and Vashishtha proposed Kushadhvaja’s daughters Mandavi and Shrutakirti for Bharata and Shatrughna. The families agreed.
An auspicious wedding time was chosen. Dasharatha arranged the rites for his sons and gave gifts of cows, clothing and wealth.
The Four Weddings
Each of the four couples remains distinctly identified.
Bharata’s maternal uncle Yudhajit also reached Mithila. Having heard about his nephews in Ayodhya, he came for the weddings.
Before the sacred fire, Janaka placed Sita’s hand in Rama’s. They performed the marriage rites.
Janaka
Sita will be your companion in dharma.
Lakshmana took Urmila’s hand. They circled the sacred fire and received their elders’ blessings.
Bharata married Mandavi, joining the families of Janaka and Kushadhvaja through another bond.
Shatrughna married Shrutakirti. With all four brothers married, joy filled the assembly.
The four couples circled the sacred fire and their elders, receiving blessings. Amid auspicious sounds, both families celebrated.
Parashurama’s Challenge
A new encounter on the journey home after the weddings.
The next morning, Vishwamitra blessed the kings and princes and departed for the Himalayas. Dasharatha’s party began the journey to Ayodhya.
Ominous signs and a fierce storm arose on the road. Through it came Jamadagni’s son Parashurama, carrying a bow and an axe.
Parashurama told the history of the bows of Shiva and Vishnu. His Vaishnava bow was different from Shiva’s bow, broken in Mithila.
Dasharatha pleaded for his sons’ safety. Parashurama addressed Rama directly and issued his challenge.
Dasharatha
Please grant my sons safety.
Parashurama asked Rama to fit an arrow to this bow and prove his strength. He then wished to challenge Rama to a duel.
Parashurama
Show me that you can fit an arrow to this bow.
Rama’s Answer with the Bow
Courage tempered by respect and restraint.
Rama had remained silent out of respect for his father. Honouring Parashurama, he asked not to be regarded as powerless.
Rama
Now you shall see my strength.
Rama took the Vaishnava bow, strung it and fitted an arrow. Recognizing his radiance, Parashurama began to grow calm.

Rama spared Parashurama as a Brahmin and a relative of Vishwamitra. For the arrow’s target, he offered a choice: his swift movement or the worlds earned by austerity. Parashurama chose to relinquish those worlds.
Parashurama
Let the worlds I have earned be your target.
Rama released the arrow. Parashurama acknowledged his greatness, circled him respectfully and left for Mount Mahendra.
Return to Ayodhya
Bālakāṇḍa ends here; the exile has not yet begun.
Rama entrusted the Vaishnava bow to Varuna. Dasharatha embraced him, and the party resumed its journey to Ayodhya.
Ayodhya was decorated for celebration. Kaushalya, Sumitra and Kaikeyi welcomed Sita, Urmila, Mandavi and Shrutakirti.
Some time later, with their parents’ permission, Bharata and Shatrughna went with their uncle Yudhajit to their maternal family’s home.
Rama and Lakshmana served the people under their father’s guidance. Rama and Sita’s affection deepened. Here the story of Bālakāṇḍa ends.
